en: The *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra* composed by the most learned Śrī Vāmana, together with its own commentary (*svavṛtti*).
The first chapter of the first section, titled "The Body" (Śārīra). Having prostrated before the Supreme Light, Vāmana [composed] this work dear to poets.
A commentary on those *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtras* is now being composed.
Poetry is to be accepted for its ornamentation.
Beauty is the ornament. (VKal 1.1.2)
It [is established] through the abandonment of faults and the adoption of virtues and ornaments.
According to the treatise, they are as follows.
Poetry has both visible and invisible purposes,
because it is the cause of pleasure and fame.
// VKal 1.1.5 // Chapter Two.
The wise are those who suffer from loss of appetite and who consume even grass.
The former are disciples because of their discernment;
the others are not, because of the opposite.
Scripture is not purposeful with regard to non-substantial entities.
The clearing-nut is not for the purpose of purifying mud.
Style is the soul of poetry.
Rīti is a distinguished arrangement of words.
The particularity consists of the qualities.
It is threefold: Vaidarbhī, Gauḍīyā, and Pāñcālī.
It is designated by that name because it is observed in Vidarbha and other such regions.
Vaidarbhi is endowed with all [these] qualities.
The Gauḍīya style possesses vitality and beauty.
The Pāñcālī style is endowed with sweetness and delicacy.
Among them, the first should be accepted because of its completeness of qualities; not, however, the others.
Because its qualities are few.
Some say that there is practice with the other [two] for the sake of ascending it.

But that is not so; for one whose character is not grounded in reality cannot achieve reality. (VKal 1.2.17) Just as by the practice of weaving hemp thread, one does not obtain the variety of weaving fine silk thread. (VKal 1.2.18)
That too, in the absence of compounds, is the pure Vaidarbhī style.
In that [work], the excellence of the qualities of meaning is to be savored.
From ascending that [ladder], there is even a slight portion of the qualities of the goal.
She too is Vaidarbhī,
by virtue of residing therein.
// [End of] the Third Chapter.
The world, knowledge, and miscellaneous topics are the auxiliary limbs of poetry.
The world's conduct is the world itself.
The sciences preceded by grammar, lexicography, dictionaries, prosody, the arts, the treatises on love, and the science of government (are the first group). VKal_1,3.3 //
From the recollection of words comes the purity of words.
The determination of the meaning of words is derived from a lexicon.
The *Chandoviciti* is for the purpose of cutting through doubts regarding metrical feet.
From the arts and sciences arises the consciousness of the principle of art (kalātattva).
From the science of love (kāmaśāstra), [one learns] the practice of love (kāmopacāra).
The science of government consists of policy and its opposite.
And from that, there arises the crookedness of what has occurred.
Knowledge of the target, diligent application, service to the elders, observation, intuition, and attentiveness constitute miscellaneous [qualities]. (VKal 1.3.11)
In this context, familiarity with poetry consists in the knowledge of its defining characteristics.
The effort toward the composition of poetry is *abhiyoga*.
Service to the teacher who instructs one in poetry is service to the elders.
The laying down of the foot, the lifting up, and the looking.
The seed of poetry is creative intuition (*pratibhāna*).
One-pointedness of mind is attentiveness.
That [is established] by means of place and time. (VK 1.3.18)
A secluded place. VKal_1,3.19.
The fourth watch of the night is the time [for this].
Poetry consists of both prose and verse.
Prose that has the scent of verse, as well as that which is like powder and abounds in ripples (waves).
That which possesses the scent of meter, like the portion of a verse, is called *vṛttagandhi*.
The *cūrṇa* (powdered verse) has feet that are neither displaced nor overly ornate.
The opposite [of that] consists primarily of agitation.
Padya has many varieties.
That is both unbound and bound.
The establishment of their sequence is like that of a garland and its crest-ornament.
An unbound [entity] does not shine, like a single atom of light.
Among literary compositions, the *daśarūpaka* (the ten types of drama) is the most excellent.
For that [cognition] is variegated, like a variegated cloth, because of the completeness of its particulars.
From that, the postulation of other distinctions [arises].
And thus concludes this first section, the "Investigation of the Body.
[Now begins] the second section, named "Observation of Faults," Chapter One.
Defects are of the nature of the reversal of qualities.
The comprehension of that [meaning] occurs through the sense. 2.1.2.
The elaboration is for the sake of ease.
A faulty word is one that is unskillful, harsh, vulgar, unintelligible, or meaningless.
That which contradicts the traditional memory of words is incorrect.
It is disagreeable to the Vedas and painful.
That which is employed merely for worldly purposes is the vulgar (grāmya).
That which is employed solely by the treatise is "unrecognized."
That which is for the sake of filling [the meter] is meaningless.
Nor for the purpose of embellishing the sentence. (VKal 2.1.10)
And those that have a different meaning, are lead elsewhere, possess a hidden meaning, are indecorous, and are obscure. (VKal 2.1.11)
That which has fallen from its conventional usage and possesses another meaning [is called *yogarūḍha*].
That which has a conceptualized object is of interpretable meaning.
That which employs words whose meanings are not well-known is "obscure" (gūḍhārtha).
Vulgar speech is that which has no connection to the subject matter and serves as a cause for improper recollection.
They are not concealed, characterized, or restrained.
A secret [transaction] is one that is not known to the members of the assembly. // VKal_2,1.17 //
That which is endowed with characteristic and non-refined [elements] is the "defined" (lakṣita).
Enveloped by the world means being concealed.
The threefold nature of tantra arises from its divisions, which produce shame, disgust, inauspiciousness, and terror.
(VKal 2.1.20) That which conveys a meaning through mediation is "afflicted" (*kliṣṭa*). (VKal 2.1.21)
The sentence has been explained by means of the last two [verses]. // VKal_2,1.22 // @-------------------- Second Chapter:
Sentences with broken meters, lost caesuras, and faulty sandhis. // VKal_2,2.1 //
That which has deviated from its own characteristic and fallen away from its proper conduct is "one of broken conduct."
That which lacks heroic sentiment and is devoid of pause is "fallen from the caesura" (yatibhraṣṭa).
In the division of the parts of those stems and names, this generally applies when vowel sandhi has not been performed.
The pause (*yati*) is not distinct from the metrical foot (*vṛtta*), because the metrical foot consists of the pause.
[Objection: No, because their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are distinct. *Vajrakalpa* 2.2.5–2.2.6.
A hiatus between words that is discordant due to their irregular form is *visaṃdhi*.
The defects of the junction between words are irregularity, disjunction, vulgarity, and harshness.
[These are] the useless, the single-meaning, the doubtful, the illogical, the out-of-order, and those contradictory to worldly convention and to science. (VKal_2.2.9)
That whose preceding and succeeding meanings are contradictory is "meaningless" (vyartha).
A word whose meaning has already been stated is one that has the same meaning [as the preceding word]. // VKal_2.2.11 //

No; for if there is a distinction, then the single referent is defective. (VKal 2.2.12) The word "bow" [is used] for the bowstring and the path in order to convey the sense of being strung. (VKal 2.2.13)
The designation of "ear" and so forth in the expressions "ear-ornament," "ear-ring," and "head-garland" is due to their proximity [to those parts].
In the compound "muktāhāra," the word *muktā* [is used] because of its purity.
In the compound "puṣpamālā" (flower-garland), the word "puṣpa" (flower) [expresses] excellence.
In the expression "young elephant" (*karikalabha*), the word "elephant" (*kari*) [denotes its meaning] through identity (*tādrūpya*).
And [the same applies] to the qualifier.
This [is the case] regarding those who have applied themselves [to practice]. // VKal_2,2.19 //
That which creates doubt is "doubtful. (VKal 2.20)
It is employed for the sake of objects conceptualized as illusions and the like.
That which lacks the proper sequence is called *apakrama*, meaning "out of order."
Those whose meanings contradict place, time, and intrinsic nature are contradictory to the world.
Those meanings which contradict the treatises on the arts and the four aims of human life are contrary to knowledge. (VKal_2.24)
This second section, titled "The Observation of Faults," is concluded.
Now begins the third section, titled "The Discrimination of Qualities," Chapter One.
The qualities (guṇas) are those properties that produce the beauty of poetry.
The causes of that excellence are the poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra).
The former are eternal.

Vigor (ojas), clarity (prasāda), cohesion (śleṣa), evenness (samatā), concentration (samādhi), sweetness (mādhurya), delicacy (saukumārya), loftiness (audāratā), explicitness of meaning (arthavyakti), and beauty (kānti) are the qualities of composition (bandhaguṇa).
Ojas is the state of being firmly bound.
Laxity is serenity.
There is an accumulation of merit due to the convergence [of means].
But that [self] is established by experience.
And [it consists of] equality and superiority. 3.1.9.
Smoothness is cohesion.
The non-confusion regarding the path is equanimity.
The sequence of ascent and descent is meditative absorption (samādhi).
They are not distinct, because *ojas* (vitality) and *prasāda* (clarity) consist of the ascending and descending [movements].
// VKal_3,1.13 //* No, because they are unmixed. // VKal_3,1.14 //* And because [the reason] is inconclusive. // VKal_3,1.15 //*
If it is accepted that those two are the intense states of *ojas* and *prasāda*,
[it is so] because they depend upon specific conditions. (VKal 3.1.16–17)
Concentration is said to be the cause for ascending and descending.
Or [it is] for the purpose of establishing the sequence.
Sweetness (*mādhurya*) consists in the distinctness of words (*pṛthakpadatva*).
Tenderness is the state of being free from coarseness.
Vikaṭatva (monstrosity) is udāratā (loftiness).
The state of being the cause for the manifestation of meaning is "manifestation of meaning" (*arthavyakti*).
Brilliance is luster. (VKal 3.1.24)
They are not non-existent, because they are experienced as being existent.
They are not erroneous,
because they are unshakable.
The properties [of words] are not those of the recitation,
because they are not observed everywhere. // VKal 3.1.27 //
— Second Chapter —
These very things are the qualities of the meaning.
The maturity of meaning is *ojas*.
Clarity is the purity of the meaning.
The occurrence [of these] is *śleṣa* (punning condensation). // VKal_3.2.4 //
Absence of inequality is equanimity.
The vision of the object is meditative concentration.
The object is of two kinds:
that which is not born from another, or that which is born from the shadow of another.
The object is both manifest and subtle.
It is subtle, to be cultivated, and to be permeated by habitual tendencies.
Sweetness is the variety of expression.
Absence of harshness is gentleness.
The state of being non-vulgar is nobility (audārya).
The manifestation of the object is the clarity of the intrinsic nature of the thing.
Lustre is the state of having radiant flavor.
Thus concludes the third chapter, the Analysis of the Qualities (*guṇavivecana*). The Fourth Chapter, titled "Poetics" (*ālaṅkārika*),
First Section.
Yamaka consists of a word, a non-synonymous phrase, or a syllable that is repeated according to a fixed position.
The feet are the initial, middle, and final portions of one foot or of many; these are the positions.
From dissolution comes excellence.
The chain, the turner, and the powder—this is the path of breaking.
The breaking and shifting of phonemes is the *śṛṅkhalā*.
The "transformer" (parivartaka) is the attainment of one's true nature upon the cessation of attachment.
When there is a division of the *piṇḍa* and the syllables, the loss of its own form is the *cūrṇa*.
Alliteration is the repetition of similar sounds in the remainder [of the verse].
Alliteration that is not coarse is superior.
Pādānuprāsa (alliteration within the quarters) is like pādayamaka (rhyme between quarters). [End of Chapter 4, Section 1] Chapter Two.
Upamā (simile) is the similarity of the object of comparison (*upameya*) with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), based on even a slight degree of common quality. [VKal_4,2.1]
And it is designated as such due to the abundance of its qualities. // VKal_4.2.2 //
That [metaphor] is of two kinds,
due to the distinction between its occurrence in the meaning of a word or the meaning of a sentence. It is either complete (*pūrṇā*) or elliptical (*luptā*).
When there is the totality of words expressing the quality, the standard of comparison, and the object of comparison, it is the complete simile (pūrṇopamā).
When there is an elision, it is called *luptā*.
In the recounting of praise, blame, and reality.
The defects of that [comparison] are inferiority, superiority, difference in gender and number, dissimilarity, and impossibility. // VKal_4.2.8 //
Inferiority of a comparison consists in its being deficient in terms of genus, measure, or quality.
When one of two things is mentioned, there is a cognition of the other due to their constant association.
By this, the case of the remainder is explained.
The difference in gender (*liṅgabheda*) refers to the transposition of gender between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*).
It is generally desired in both the masculine and neuter genders.
In the worldly [use of language], when expressed through compounds, and in the manifold varieties of similes.
By this, the distinction between types of speech is explained.
Non-similarity is the non-existence of a similarity with a quality that has not been perceived.
For comparison is destroyed by dissimilarity, and poets are devoted to that [comparison].
Some say that its exclusion occurs due to the superiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). (VKal 4.2.17–18)
No, because the meaning is not supported.
Non-occurrence is impossibility.
There is no contradiction regarding the excellence. // VKal_4.2.21 // @-------------------- Third Chapter: The Elaboration of Similes, beginning with *prativastu* and so forth. // VKal_4.3.1 //
When the object of comparison is mentioned, the presentation of a corresponding thing is *prativastūpamā*.
When [the object of comparison] is not explicitly stated, it is *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression).
When something is mentioned, it may be *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
Apahnuti (concealment) is the denial of one thing by means of another similar object.
Metaphor (*rūpaka*) is the superimposition of identity upon the object of comparison (*upameya*) due to the equality of its qualities with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
He is one who possesses mastery in the application of the methods within the teachings.
Metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on similarity is *vakrokti* (indirect expression).
Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is the determination of something as having a nature other than its own, for the sake of intensification.
Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is the conceptualization of an excellence that exceeds the possible nature of things.
The figure of speech *saṃdeha* (doubt) consists of a doubt regarding the object of comparison and the subject of comparison.
Contradiction is the state of having contradictory appearances.
Vibhāvanā is the manifestation of a well-known result despite the negation of the action that produces it. (VKal 4.3.13)
When a single thing functions as both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, it is *ananvaya* (non-correspondence).
Successive Simile (kramopamā) is when there is a comparison of the subject with the object [and then that object with the subject].
Parivṛtti (exchange) is the substitution of two things that are either equal or dissimilar. // VKal_4,3.16 //
Krama (sequence) is the sequential connection between the objects of comparison and the standards of comparison.
When there is a single verb in sentences containing both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, it is *dīpaka*.

The tantra is threefold, due to the distinction between the modes of expression in its beginning, middle, and end. (VKal 4.3.19) An illustration (*nidarśana*) is the manifestation of the connection between itself and its own meaning through action alone. (VKal 4.3.20)
Arthāntaranyāsa is the presentation of a different matter (arthāntara) for the sake of establishing a statement regarding a given subject. // VKal_4,3.21 //
Vyatireka (distinction) is the superiority of the qualities of the object of comparison.
When there is a conceptualization of the loss of even a single quality [of one thing] while another remains equal, it is *viśeṣokti* (the description of distinction). // VKal 4.3.23 //
Vyājastuti (ironical praise) consists of censure or praise intended for a specific purpose, arising from the non-performance of a distinguished action that would otherwise be expected. VKal_4,3.24.
Vyājokti (the figure of speech of "disguise") is the resemblance of a pretext to the truth.
Equal pairing (*tulyayogitā*) is the conjunction of actions at the same time for the purpose of equating that which is distinguished with something else.
And the rejection of a simile is also *ākṣepa*.
*Saṃhokti* (concomitance) is the expression by a single word of two things or two actions occurring at the same time. // VKal_4,3.28 //
That which is similarity is its perfection; it is composed.
The state of one ornament being the source of another ornament is *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling).
Its two varieties are Simile (upamā) and Metaphor (rūpaka), as well as Poetic Fancy (utprekṣā) and its parts (avayava).
The metaphorical simile (upamārūpaka) is a metaphor (rūpaka) produced by means of a simile (upamā).
The cause of poetic fancy (utprekṣāhetu) is a constituent part of poetic fancy (utprekṣāvayava).
Thus concludes the fourth section, the *Ālaṅkārika*.
The fifth section, named the *Prāyogika*,
Chapter One.
Generally, a single word should not be used twice. (VKal 5.1.1)
The *saṃhitā* is constant throughout the quarters of the verse, as if it were a single word, except at the end of the half-verse.
And there is no heaviness for a light syllable at the end of a foot in all cases.

In the Gāthā meter, the *vṛtta* is almost complete, except for the *udgata* and others due to their correspondence [with other meters]. // VKal_5,1.4 //* Nor should particles such as *khalu* and so forth appear at the beginning of a quarter-verse. // VKal_5,1.5 //*
No sentence is completed with only half [a word]. (VKal 5.1.6)
A *karmadhāraya* compound does not bring about the understanding of a *bahuvrīhi*.
By this, the opposite case has been explained.
In the negation of a possible negation, there are two negations.
The employment of the qualifier alone [is sufficient] when the qualified object is already understood.
The connection [of a word] concealed by a compound occurs through a pronoun.
In some cases, the genitive case is used even for a relation of a relation.
A word from the local dialect that is excessively employed.
The supplying of ellipses and the supplying of words based on indicative marks.
And words [functioning] by way of indication (lakṣaṇā). VKal 5.1.15.
There is no abundance of that in one place.
In most cases, the genus (*jāti*) of the breasts and so forth is entered into by duality (*dvitva*).
[End of Chapter 5, Verse 17] **Second Chapter:** The *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) as "the two Rudras" (*rudrau*) is to be sought. [End of Chapter 5, Verse 1]
The status of *dhātu* for [roots] such as *mil*, *klab*,
and *kṣip* is due to the non-completion of the quality (*guṇa*) of a *dhātu*. The *ātmanepada* [suffix] after the root *val* is not obligatory.
On account of the indicator (*jñāpaka*).
[The form] "it is diminished" (*kṣīyate*) is used in the sense of the object acting as its own agent (*karmakartṛ*).
And "he becomes weary" (khidyate). // VKal_5.2.5 //
The path is the stainless mark of the self.
And [the suffix] *ānaś* is used after [roots] such as *lol* (to roll) and others.

Because the root *labh* has the sense of "going" (*gaty-artha*), when it is in the causative (*ṇic*) and the non-causative (*aṇ*), there is the status of object (*karman*) or non-object (*akarmatva*) for the agent (*kartṛ*).
The words *te* and *me* are included among the indeclinables (*nipāta*).
In the sense of "disregarded," it means "overcome" (*paribhūta*), due to the figurative application (*upacāra*) of the term "interior" (*antardhi*).
It is not a single word, because it is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4).
[The compound] *madhupipāsu* and others are established as compounds because they are included in the list beginning with *gami-gāmī* (Pāṇini 2.1.70).
The word *trivalī* is established [as a valid form] if it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*).
In the compound *bimbādhara*, the middle term is elided according to the rule of *madhyamapadalopī* (elision of the middle member).
The occurrence [of the suffix] after words such as *āmūla* and *lola* is like that of *vispaṣṭa* and *paṭu*.
There is no prohibition of the *ṣaṣṭhī*-compound in cases such as *dhānya-ṣaṣṭha* and so forth,
because it ends in a *taddhita* suffix [denoting] a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*).
[The prohibition applies] in cases such as *patra-pītima* and so forth, because [the second member] is a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*).
A bahuvrīhi compound whose final member is "janman" (birth) or similar terms is not to be avoided even when it has non-co-referential members.
The "hand-tip" and "tip-of-hand" and so forth [are used] because of the difference-in-identity between quality and the possessor of the quality.
In the case of a preceding placement [of a word], the corruption must be guarded against.

Even when the object (*karman*) is expressed by a particle (*nipāta*), the case-ending for the object does not occur, because the specific enumeration [of such particles] is merely illustrative (*prāyika*). (VKal 5.2.21) The form *śakyam* expresses the object; furthermore, its gender and number are also [determined] by reference to the general [subject], as it begins with a general term. (VKal 5.2.22)
Just as deficiency, so too excess of the constituent parts is a disorder.
"Not [the term] *kṛmikīṭānām*," because it would result in the application of the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*).
Nor [the term] *kharoṣṭrau*.
Because of the reading "uṣṭrakharām" [it is so called];
[the form] "āsa" is derived from the root "ās" [in the sense of sitting].
The form *yudhyet* is derived from the root *yudh* with the suffix *kyac*.
The suffix *kyaṅ* should be examined in cases such as *viralāyamāna*.

In the word *ahetu*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the root *han* because it is included in the *curādi* group. (VKal 5.2.29) The form *anucarī* is derived from the root *car* with the suffix *ṭit*. (VKal 5.2.30)
The suffix *raṇi* is applied after the word *kesarāla* to form the feminine noun *kesarālī*.
The word *patrala* is derived from the root *lā* with the suffix *ke*.
The words *mahīdhra* and others [are derived with the suffix *ka*] because we observe the rule for roots such as *mūlavibhuja*.
Because the root *han* is restricted to [denoting] Brahmā and others, there is no establishment of [the meaning] "enemy" and so forth here.
The terms *brahmavid* and so forth are [formed] by means of a derivative (*kṛdanta*) function.
By these, the mountains and so forth are explained. (VKal 5.2.36)
The words beginning with *bhidura* are used in the sense of the agent as object (*karmakartṛ*) and in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The expansion of qualities and so forth are inconceivable.
The reversal of long and short vowels in the words *avatāra* and *apacāya* is a characteristic of the ignorant.
It is "śobheti" by virtue of an irregular grammatical derivation (nipātana).
In the absence of a specific rule, there is a frequent desire to express the feminine gender for a guru.
In the case of [roots] such as *vyava-si*, the suffix *kta* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), due to the inclusion of the particle *ca*.
The form *āha* occurs in the sense of the past (*bhūte*) due to a confusion with other forms ending in *ṇal*; it is used with the root *brū* in the present tense (*laṭ*).
The suffix *ṭāp* is not applicable for feminine gender after words such as *śabala*.
In the case of a living being, it should be considered as "blue."
Regarding the human species, there is both the intention to express and the lack of intention to express.
The suffix *ūṅ* also occurs after a word ending in *ū*, because it is so prescribed; thus,
*kārtikīya* [is formed] with the suffix *ṭhañ*, which is difficult to maintain [otherwise].
And [the term] "pertaining to Śarva" (śārvaram) is also used.
Because of the usage of the term "eternal" (śāśvata).
Those such as members of the royal lineage who exist for the sake of what is wholesome.
The word "dārava" is misused.
One should seek [the truth] as one does in states such as infatuation.
And [the categories] beginning with "comparison" (aupamya) are like the four castes (cāturvarṇya).
Due to the addition of the marker *ṣit* to the suffix *ṣyañ*, the long vowel *ī* occurs diversely.
The word *dhanvī* [is formed] because of its inclusion in the *vrīhyādi* group [of nominal stems].
The term "caturasraśobhī" is formed by adding the suffix *ṇini*.
The word *kañcukīya* is derived from the root *kyac*. (Pāṇini 5.2.58)
Even when there is dependence on a Buddhist counter-correlative, these are superlative suffixes.
The suffix *ilac* is applied after [stems ending in] *kauśila* and others, due to the elision of a phoneme.
It is "mauktika" because it is listed among the words beginning with "vinaya" [in the Amarakośa].
The intuitive faculty (*prātibha*) and others are included among the forms of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth.
In the case of *na sarajasam*, it is not an *avyayībhāva* compound.
When the term *dhṛtadhanuṣi* does not denote a proper name, [the suffix *cha* is applied]. (VKal 5.2.64)
The state of being free from foul odors is difficult to attain.
Those beginning with "the fair-toothed one" (sudatī) are to be understood as counter-examples.
In *kṣatadṛḍhoraḥ*, the suffix *kap* does not apply,
because of the prohibition against the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) [to the compound].
In *avaihi*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* is improper.
"One whose eyes reach to the corners" (apāṅganetra) is one who is difficult to obtain. (VKal 5.2.69)
*Neṣṭāḥ śliṣṭapriyādayaḥ*, because of the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).
*Dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* [is used] everywhere. (VKal 5.2.71)
The *jambulatā* and others are [the result] of the rule for short vowels.
The *tilaka* and other [ornaments] are [applied] on the forehead and other [parts of the body].
The two words *niśamya* and *niśamayya* arise from a difference in their verbal roots.

The words *saṃyamya* and *niyamya* [are derived] from the root *yam* with the suffix *lyap*, because it does not take the causative (*ṇic*) affix. // VKal 5.2.75 // *Prapīya* is derived from the root *pīṅ*. // VKal 5.2.76 //
It means "it causes to go far away," due to the inclusion of the term *bahula* (in the rule).
The augment *num* is not prohibited after [a stem ending in] *gacchati* and similar forms.
In the case of *mitreṇa* and *goptreṇa*, the masculine form is applied due to the rule of *puṃvadbhāva*.
"You shall find [it]"—this is due to the breaking of the word (*padabhanga*).
If the word *kāmayāna* is established as being beginningless, [then it is valid].
The words *sauhṛda* and *daurhṛda* are formed from the root *hṛ* with the suffix *aṇ*.
This is due to the irregular grammatical formation (*nipātana*) of the word *virama*.
When words such as *upari* and others are repeated in the sense of proximity, the second case ending is used.
"Slowly, slowly" is used when there is no specific purpose [for the action]. (VKal_5,2.85)
In *na nidrādrug*,
the change to *bhaṣ* has been attained;
in *niṣpanda*, the substitution of *patva* should be considered.
"There is no joining of the fingers" refers to the rule concerning the crown of the head.
By this, Āvantisena and others have been answered.
There is no substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *indravāhana*,
because the state of being "placed upon" (*āhitatva*) is not intended to be expressed.
Thus ends this fifth section concerning practical application (*prāyogika*).
This work is completed.
